To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

distinctive and replicably abnormal neurometric profiles are associated with the DSM-III-R clinical diagnoses, and that these clinical diagnoses are not the best way to group patients for treatment purposes.

(1) QEEG variables can be used to distinguish psychiatric patients from normals, and (2) patients in different diagnostic categories can be distinguished from one another using the same set of QEEG variables.

distinctive neurometric abnormalities in QEEG are found to be associated with the symptom clusters upon which the DSM-III-R psychiatric diagnoses are based, that the pathophysiology of patients in each DSM-III-R category is heterogeneous, and that patients from different categories may have similar pathophysiology.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a taxonomy of neuropsychiatric disorders, based upon the identification of pathophysiological patterns of brain electrical activity.

the use of QEEG as a quantitative measure of brain function in the study of psychiatric disorders, with the ultimate objective of developing a biological basis for the classification and treatment of psychiatric disorders.
the development of objective methods to classify psychiatric patients, based on physiological measurements of the brain’s electrical activity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the QEEG is an excellent and sensitive measure of brain function, and that it is useful in the study of psychiatric disorders.
the present study provides evidence of the existence of subtypes of psychiatric disorders which are not reflected in DSM-III-R.

there is a ‘natural’ structure in the population of psychiatric patients which is not reflected in the diagnostic categories of DSM-III-R, and which is not reflected by any of the clinical measures used in this study.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
neurometric abnormalities in QEEG are correlated with clinical diagnoses, and may provide useful information for treatment planning.

QEEG can provide information useful in the classification of psychiatric disorders, and that this classification can be improved by using cluster analysis to subdivide the patients into subgroups with similar pathophysiology.

neurometric Q-EEG variables are sensitive to the pathophysiology of psychiatric disorders and may be used to identify subtypes of patients with the same diagnosis who may respond differently to the same treatment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the QEEG data can be used to classify psychiatric patients into subtypes that have similar patterns of brain activity and may respond similarly to treatment.
the brain is not a unitary organ and that different brain systems may be involved in the production of different psychiatric symptoms.
QEEG may be useful to identify patients who may benefit from different treatments, even if they have the same DSM-III-R diagnosis.
